brief.head: Brains, not stomachs
brief.text: Indians are taught at school that population is the country’s biggest problem. Amit Varma disagrees: people are brains, not stomachs, and what gets blamed on numbers is failed governance. {001-C05}

brief.head: Rather be poor where?
brief.text: Would you rather be poor in the USA or Bangladesh? Everyone picks the USA, Amit Varma said, though it is more unequal. India’s problem is poverty, not inequality. {001-C06}

brief.head: Old songs, new sales
brief.text: Old music now outsells new, Amit Varma reported. Ajay Shah doubted that tastes fixed in youth explain it: *Dark Side of the Moon* remains among the most successful albums ever. {001-C14}

brief.head: Oral history
brief.text: *The Seen and the Unseen*, Amit Varma’s other podcast, has become oral history, Ajay Shah said: deep dives of three to eight hours into one interesting person at a time. {001-R22}

brief.head: Uncles only
brief.text: Only men can be uncles, Amit Varma conceded while explaining the compliment he had been paid. Women, he suggested, “can be Karens, I guess.” {001-J05}

thought.text: Books offer you not an escape from life but an embrace of it.

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah begin a weekly conversation
lead.head: Of snakes, seagulls and uncles
body: The first episode of *Everything is Everything* began with a promise and a haircut. Amit Varma said the new weekly show would talk “not just about the profound, but also the profane”. Ajay Shah asked at once how he got that interesting haircut. {001-J01}
It was the village barber’s work, done with no electricity.
The thread through what followed was the image that gives the episode its title: people as works in progress, halfway from coal and halfway to diamond, able to rewrite themselves.
## The cobra and the code

Shah’s subject was animals. India’s big four venomous snakes, he said, are very different from one another. The cobra lives around people, flashes its hood and often strikes with its mouth closed: it is “much less dangerous than is widely considered”.
Seagulls are the reverse: graceful to look at, they kill pigeons and gouge chunks from the backs of baby whales.

We pass no moral judgment on animals, Varma observed, though humans, also animals, are judged for everything. Shah’s answer was hardware and software. A newborn king cobra is hard-coded for life; humans run an operating system of culture that they can examine and rewrite. “So culture, that plasticity is what makes us human,” he said. {001-C01}
Varma replied that character is contingent, shaped by genes and circumstances. But even if there is no free will, he argued, “for civilization to progress, we must behave as if there is.” {001-C02}
Shah’s rule for the striving in between was to judge the algorithm, not the outcome: “don’t judge a decision by its outcome because the world is probabilistic.” {001-C03}
## Uncles and anti-uncles
Varma’s subject began with a compliment. The writer Shrayana Bhattacharya once told him he was an “anti-uncle”: open to ideas, ready to change his mind and to engage with anyone. {001-S05}

That led Varma to Paul Graham’s essay *The Four Quadrants of Conformism*. The aggressively conventional-minded make the loudest noise on social media without saying anything new, Varma said, and they hold back progress. {001-C04}

Shah, by his own description a “card carrying economist”, was kinder. “People are not wood, people are not stones, people are optimizers,” he said. {001-C07} Many uncles, in his view, ride an ideology towards power and will turn on a dime.

He cited his old teacher Timur Kuran’s idea of preference falsification: before communism fell, everyone in East Germany and the USSR professed the official beliefs, and in their hearts nobody held them. {001-C08}
Criticism, Shah added, suffers from a market failure. The critic takes the attacks, while the progress belongs to everyone.
## A life in every book
Books, Varma argued, let us collect far more dots than experience does, and fiction lets us live other lives. Shah added that every great book of ideas gives its reader one extra life.

The hosts ended on a puzzle. Far more people today can make art or do science than ever before, so where are the masterpieces? Funding for science has risen a millionfold, Shah said, and yet “something about the machine, something about the modern world, is interfering with the great leaps.” {001-C15}
All that money, he grumbled, had produced food delivery apps and LLMs. Varma’s remedy: uninstall the apps and cook our own food.
Varma, new to video, joked that he has “a face for audio”. {001-J12}

second.label: Luck and art
second.head: Play it again, please
second.deck: Amit Varma on the listener who talked Billy Joel’s song onto the radio
body: Billy Joel’s *Piano Man* almost disappeared into oblivion, Amit Varma said, and Joel was not going to make any more music. {001-S09}

Then one man who loved the song went from radio station to radio station, asking them to play it. At a big station he finally struck a deal with someone, and “almost bribed him in a sense”, Varma said. The song went on air and became a hit, and Joel went on to make many more albums.
Varma told the story to show how much luck decides which art survives. Bach, he noted, only became a big name decades after his death. {#bach}

quote.text: So there’s so much luck involved as well.

second.caption: the fan who saved “Piano Man”

third.head: Blame the macroeconomists
body: Why is old music outselling new? Ajay Shah has a half-joking theory: it is all the fault of the macroeconomists.

They conquered business cycles, he said, and Robert Lucas famously declared after the response to the 2008 crisis that “we won”. {#lucas} “The Great Depression gave us Adolf Hitler. The 2008 crisis only gave us Donald Trump,” Shah said. {001-J10}
Music, he argued, needed the angst and misery of bad times as fuel, so great music would now come from Russia, China and the horrible places of the world.

Amit Varma said they were fortunate to have escaped such times, though many people in India still live through them. Shah pointed to Rabindranath Tagore, personally privileged but wired into a difficult time, and concluded that good art may be counter-cyclical. {001-C13}
third.caption: why good times make bad music

p2.deck: Snakes, uncles, books and bands: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on how people grow, and what stops them {001-C03}

sections.label: Nature and nurture
sections.head: Code we can rewrite
sections.caption: culture as a human operating system
body: Animals do brutal things, and nobody judges them for it. Seagulls, Ajay Shah said, kill pigeons, and have been reported gouging out the eyes of seals. {001-S04}

Yet humans are animals too, Amit Varma observed, and everything they do is morally judged. Much of what we call reasoning is really rationalisation for wherever our instincts take us. He quoted Steven Pinker: “Nature gives us knobs, nurture turns them.” {001-J14}
## Hardware and software

Shah saw a deeper difference. A newborn king cobra is a hundred per cent king cobra at birth: it can bite and kill, and its code stays the same for the rest of its life. Humans add an operating system of culture, learned behaviours, beliefs and heuristics, and are unique in being able to interrogate and modify it. {001-C01}

Varma took the metaphor as support for his own point: character is contingent. Still, a society needs an ethical code that punishes the bad and rewards the good, he said, so we must behave as if people are responsible even if, at the deepest level, they are not. {001-C02}
~ Shah settled on shades of grey. We are each works in progress, he said; when an event ambushes us we act on instinct, and growth lies in asking afterwards whether that instinct was right. {001-C03}

quote.text: We are masters of our own destiny because to some extent we’re able to interrogate and modify that operating system.

sections.label: Uncle watch
sections.head: The call of the uncle
sections.caption: uncles, anti-uncles and Galileo’s defiance
body: The writer Shrayana Bhattacharya once paid Amit Varma what he calls one of the finest compliments he has received: “Amit, you are an anti-uncle.” He listens to the other side; an uncle is closed and insistent on his worldview. {001-S05}

Varma found the types mapped in Paul Graham’s essay, which identifies four kinds of mind by their calls, like species of birds. The aggressively conventional-minded cry “Crush outgroup!”; the passively conventional ask what the neighbours will think; the passively independent say to each his own.

The aggressively independent say *Eppur si muove*: still it turns. Galileo said it, Varma recounted, after being forced to recant that the earth goes around the sun, looking up at the sky and stamping the ground. {001-S06}
## Loud and unoriginal
The aggressively conventional-minded, whether right-wingers or wokes, make the loudest noise on social media, Varma said, and stand in the way of progress. {001-C04}
His own provocative columns had drawn them out, among them his argument that population is not India’s problem, since people are brains, not stomachs. {001-C05}
~ His remedy starts with himself. His first response to a radically new idea used to be no, he said, so he learned to fight that, because every idea that changes the world is at first a radical idea.

quote.text: The loudest noise on Twitter and social media is actually made by the aggressively conventional-minded. These are not people saying anything new.

sections.label: Why uncles conform
sections.head: Not wood, not stones
sections.caption: uncles as optimisers, not true believers
body: Ajay Shah, a self-described card-carrying economist, looks at uncles as optimisers. People want the warmth of tribal networks, he said, and loudly enforcing social norms is a ticket to power and success. {001-C07}

Many uncles, in his view, are not deep believers but are riding an ideology, and will turn on a dime when the world changes. So he is kind to them. Amit Varma accepted that as an explanation, not a justification, since social media amplifies everything.
## Private truths

Shah drew on Timur Kuran’s preference falsification. Three months before communism collapsed, everyone in East Germany and the USSR professed the official beliefs, and nobody held them; some went along passively, others aggressively policed violators. {001-C08}

Varma reached for Kuran’s other phrase, the preference cascade, to explain the Modi wave. Indian society, he argued, has always been deeply illiberal, and social media showed closet bigots that many others shared their views, so they no longer needed to hide them.
Shah, who stays away from social media entirely, separated two questions: what should I do, and how is this phenomenon acting upon the world? {001-C10}
~ Criticism, Shah added, suffers from a market failure: the critic pays a very high cost while creating a positive externality for the world. {001-C09}

quote.text: But it was wise and efficient to say that as a way to get along, as a way to gain power.

sections.label: The reading life
sections.head: One life is not enough
sections.caption: the extra lives that books give us
body: We make sense of the world by connecting dots, Amit Varma said. Personal experience gives us very few, over many years; books give us many dots very fast, and fiction lets us live the lives of others.

His pick was Mark Haddon’s *The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time*, ostensibly a murder mystery told by a 15-year-old boy. Varma read out Haddon’s description of it as “a novel about difference, about being an outsider”. {001-R01}

Thomas Nagel’s essay *What Is It Like to Be a Bat?* argued that we can describe how a bat navigates by echolocation but can never imagine it. {001-R05} With other people, Varma said, we do imagine, and mirror neurons wire us to empathise.
## An extra life

Ajay Shah extended the argument beyond fiction. The great non-fiction books are each the trajectory of one life, he said, so reading one is like living an extra life, the opposite of the practitioner who lives the same day over and over.
~ Varma also rejected the claim that people no longer read. There are moments of short attention spans, he said, but we all crave depth.

quote.text: I am made of all those books.

sections.label: Artists in amber
sections.head: Same song, older band
sections.caption: artists frozen in one old hit
body: Ajay Shah’s music pick was U2’s *Songs of Surrender*, 40 songs, mostly old, reimagined in a more grown-up way, with new arrangements and edited lyrics. It is not a formula, he said, as *MTV Unplugged* is. {001-R02}
He liked the thought that some young listeners might start here and only later go back to *The Joshua Tree*.

Amit Varma saw a larger point. Artists are forced to ossify into one static version of themselves. Radiohead, he said, are sick of performing *Creep*, written when they were immature young men. {001-J21}

A big hit can be a curse, he said, echoing the musician Gaurav Chintamani: you have changed, but “you’re ossified into that one three-minute package thing that you did twenty years ago.” {001-C12} Today bands can meet fans on Discord and change a song from day to day.
## No crossing twice
Shah applied the idea to people: no man can cross the same river twice. {001-J19} When people are held to one crystalline conception of an idea, he said, it is not fair to their own journey.
~ The Gandhi of 1919, he pointed out, was very different from the Gandhi of 1939. {#gandhi}

quote.text: No man can cross the same river twice. He’s not the same and the river is not the same.

side.boxText: Paul Graham’s *The Four Quadrants of Conformism* sorts people into conventional-minded and independent-minded, each passive or aggressive. Amit Varma called it one of the finest essays he has read in recent years, by “such a wonderful essay writer”. {001-R03}

contQuote.text: Because the critic personally takes the brunt of all the attacks that come by. But actually all the progress of the world is only made possible by the critics.

stories.caption: the snake’s tail
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s run-in with village life
stories.head: Fear finds a fifth gear
body: Amit Varma, a city slicker by his own account, has lately been living in a village, in a district he won’t name. The village barber had already taken the sides of his head. Then came the snake.

He was taking rounds of Ajay Shah’s walking track and had almost run 7 km, walking and running by turns. He was completely tired, and on the last stretch he thought he could not possibly go any faster. {#sevenk}
As he was cooling down, a snake whizzed out of the bushes on his right and into the bushes on his left. There it waited, its tail hanging out on the path.

Had it disappeared, Varma said, he would simply have carried on. But the tail reminded him of an Amitabh Bachchan and Shashi Kapoor film in which the two, bathing naked, are surprised by a woman at the door and cover the wrong part. “I thought this is a stupid snake, it thinks I can’t see it, but the tail is there.” {001-J02}
Then came a second thought: “play it safe, boy.” He turned around and sprinted madly. {001-S02}
His Garmin watch put the speed at about 25 kilometres an hour, which Shah later told him is the highest speed man can attain.
~ Shah was unmoved. Varma, he said, would be a well-adjusted villager when “the tail of a snake will no longer excite peaks of physical performance.” {001-J03}
stories.why: A tired body had more in reserve than the tired mind believed. The story also previews Shah’s point that when an event ambushes us we act on instinct, and only afterwards can ask whether the instinct was right. {001-C03}
stories.postscript: Varma insists he has no pretensions of being a well-adjusted villager.

stories.caption: seagulls
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s lakeside warning about a pretty bird
stories.head: Nice bird, nasty habits
body: By a lakeside in Udaipur, Ajay Shah once gave Amit Varma some shocking news about a bird Varma thought beautiful: “Seagulls are bastards.”

Seagulls look graceful, Shah explained, and we expect some nice vegetarian bird. {001-S04} In fact they kill and eat pigeons, gouge chunks of meat from the backs of baby whales, and have been reported gouging out the eyes of seals.

Varma added that seagulls go for the eyes first, and are lazy too: they steal food from others, which is “like stealing from a thief”. {001-J04} He thought of the License Raj state taxing its own rent-seekers.
~ Shah blamed our “anthropocentric failure”: what we expect of a seagull and what it does are far apart, and the gap creates cognitive dissonance.
stories.why: We judge animals by how they look, and are unsettled when behaviour and image part ways. From there, the hosts turned to why we don’t judge animals morally but do judge humans. {001-C01}

stories.start: And and my third piece which really pissed off so many people
stories.end: But man, the flack I kind of got for this.
stories.caption: the column that riled his old schoolmates
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the price of a provocative column
stories.head: Thirty-five years, one insult
body: Amit Varma once wrote a column arguing, a bit provocatively, that it is immoral to have children. People he had not heard from since school, 35 years earlier, found him on Facebook to tell him he was an asshole. {001-S07}

The argument rests on three things we would all accept, he said: do nothing to anyone without consent, cause no one pain, and kill no one. A child is born without consent, will feel pain and will die. {001-R10}
So having children is prima facie immoral, he argued, and the argument must be tackled, though he might well do things he thinks immoral. “We are humans, we are fucked up, that’s how it is.”
~ It was one of three columns that, Varma said, drew furious responses from the aggressively conventional-minded.
stories.why: Arguing against received wisdom in public has a personal price. Ajay Shah’s point about criticism follows: the critic takes the brunt of the attacks, while the progress the critic makes possible belongs to everyone. {001-C09}

stories.start: You know, uh Hussein Haydri who has been on the scene and the unseen
stories.end: the things they feel till ultimately they don't even feel that way anymore
stories.caption: Hussain Haidry’s loneliness
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the loneliness of being mobbed online
stories.head: Alone among a thousand
body: The poet Hussain Haidry, a guest on *The Seen and the Unseen*, was once mobbed online by right-wing accounts. He felt so alone, he told Amit Varma. {001-S08}
No one called to say they were with him, or to ask how he was feeling.

Varma has been the target of right-wing mobs and woke mobs at different times, and he knows the feeling. He has many well-wishers, he said, but no one realises what you are going through when, within an hour, a thousand people are abusing you and retweeting you. {#mob}
~ Such mob behaviour, he argued, has a chilling effect on discourse: people stop saying the things they feel, until ultimately they don’t even feel that way anymore. {#chill}
stories.why: Mobs isolate their targets. Even a writer with many well-wishers can feel alone when the abuse arrives all at once, and that kind of mob behaviour, Varma argued, chills what everyone else is willing to say.
stories.postscript: Varma’s full conversation with Haidry is Episode 275 of *The Seen and the Unseen*, titled *Hindustani Musalmaan*.

quiz.q: Which of India’s big four venomous snakes strikes with no reasonable provocation, says Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: The Russell’s viper; the cobra and krait, he said, are quite mild.

quiz.q: How fast did Amit Varma’s Garmin watch say he sprinted after spotting the snake’s tail?
quiz.a: About 25 kilometres an hour, which Shah told him is the highest speed man can attain.

quiz.q: What compliment did Shrayana Bhattacharya pay Amit Varma at a book event?
quiz.a: She called him an anti-uncle: open-minded, willing to change and to engage anyone.

quiz.q: In Paul Graham’s essay, what is the call of the aggressively conventional-minded?
quiz.a: “Crush outgroup!”, alarming, Graham notes, for its exclamation point after a variable.

quiz.q: Which scholar coined “preference falsification”, the idea Ajay Shah used to explain the Soviet collapse?
quiz.a: Timur Kuran, describing beliefs professed in public but held by nobody in private.

quiz.q: Which band, according to Amit Varma, is sick of performing its early hit “Creep”?
quiz.a: Radiohead, who wrote it when they were “immature young men”, Varma said.
